questions.q: What is a golden record, as defined in this lesson?
options: The single, trusted, best-available version of a master data entity, reconciled from matched source records
A backup copy of a database stored off-site
The oldest record in a system
Any record that has never been edited
questions.explain: A golden record is the reconciled, trusted result built by comparing and merging the matched records that refer to the same real-world entity.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'just pick your most trusted system's record' is NOT the same as building a golden record?
options: Because it is actually the correct and complete approach
Because it privileges one incomplete source over the others instead of reconciling the best available information from all of them
Because trusted systems never contain accurate data
Because golden records cannot involve more than one system by definition
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that simply using one system's version, even a trusted one, ignores potentially more accurate or complete data in the other matched source records.

questions.q: How is a golden record typically assembled, according to this lesson?
options: Field by field, deciding attribute by attribute which source's value is most trustworthy
By randomly selecting one entire source record and discarding the rest
By always using the most recently created system, regardless of field
By averaging all numeric fields and ignoring text fields
questions.explain: The lesson describes assembling the golden record attribute by attribute — e.g., phone from one source, address from another — rather than wholesale copying one record.

questions.q: What is a 'virtual' golden record, and in which architecture style is it most typical?
options: A golden record that is physically stored in every source system simultaneously
A golden record computed at query time by following cross-reference links, typical of registry-style architecture
A golden record that does not actually exist and has no definition
A golden record exclusive to centralized transaction hub architecture
questions.explain: The lesson ties virtual golden records to registry style, where no central combined row is stored and the result is computed on the fly from cross-reference links.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is a golden record a one-time snapshot or a continuously-reconciled result?
options: A one-time snapshot that never changes once created
A continuously-reconciled result that updates as source systems change
It is deleted automatically after 90 days
It is only recalculated once per decade
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states a golden record is not static — a well-maintained one updates as the underlying source systems change.
